mitigations.name: NX (Non-Executable Stack)
mitigations.primitive_impact: NX prevents execution of shellcode placed on the stack. However, RIP_CONTROL itself is not blocked — RIP can still be redirected to existing executable code (e.g., ROP gadgets, libc functions). NX constrains the target of RIP redirection but does not prevent RIP_CONTROL itself.

mitigations.name: Stack Canary
mitigations.primitive_impact: No stack canary is present. Nothing detects or prevents the return address overwrite before 'ret' executes. This is a critical missing mitigation that allows RIP_CONTROL to succeed.

mitigations.name: PIE (Position Independent Executable)
mitigations.primitive_impact: Binary base address is fixed at 0x400000. All code addresses (including ROP gadgets and function addresses) are predictable. This makes RIP_CONTROL more exploitable as targets are at known fixed addresses.

mitigations.name: ASLR (libc)
mitigations.primitive_impact: Libc addresses may be randomized at runtime (depends on kernel config). This affects redirecting RIP to libc-resident code (e.g., system, one_gadget) but does not affect redirecting to binary-resident code (fixed addresses). RIP_CONTROL to binary code is unaffected.

mitigations.name: Partial RELRO
mitigations.primitive_impact: GOT is writable. Not directly relevant to RIP_CONTROL via stack overflow, but relevant for S4 exploit chain construction (GOT overwrite is possible).

primitives.notes: STACK_CONTROL is DIRECT — saved RBP is directly overwritten by the linear gets() write. The attacker controls the 8-byte value at offset 48 that becomes RBP after 'leave'. This primitive also enables stack pivot (via 'leave' setting RSP=corrupted RBP), which is relevant for S4 exploit chain construction. Verified via GDB observing RBP = 0x4242424242424242 at the ret breakpoint.

source.root_cause: gets() at 0x4005f9 writes unbounded data to [rbp-0x30], overwriting saved RBP (offset 48) and return address (offset 56). The 'ret' at 0x400604 jumps to the corrupted return address. If it points to unmapped or NX memory, SIGSEGV occurs.
source.description: Stack buffer overflow corrupts the return address. When the corrupted return address points to invalid memory (unmapped or NX-protected), the program crashes with SIGSEGV.

chain: Return address at [rbp+8] overwritten with attacker data

controlled_element.what: Program control flow — redirected to an invalid address causing SIGSEGV
controlled_element.how: gets() overwrites the return address at offset 56. When the overwritten value points to unmapped memory (e.g., 0x4141414141414141), 'ret' causes SIGSEGV.

preconditions.description: Attacker can supply stdin input exceeding 56 bytes
preconditions.necessity: Input must reach the return address at offset 56 to cause the crash.

preconditions.description: The overwritten return address points to unmapped or non-executable memory
preconditions.necessity: If the address were valid executable memory, the program would not crash (it would redirect RIP instead). CRASH specifically requires an invalid target.

verification_plan.method: Run the binary with 100 bytes of 'A' as stdin input. Observe return code = -11 (SIGSEGV).
verification_plan.environment: Linux x86-64, glibc 2.31, no PIE, no canary, NX enabled
expected_evidence: Return code = -11 (SIGSEGV) when input exceeds 56 bytes with invalid return address

mitigations.name: NX (Non-Executable Stack)
mitigations.primitive_impact: NX ensures that if the return address points to stack memory, SIGSEGV occurs (stack is non-executable). This makes the crash more likely when the attacker does not carefully choose a valid executable target.

mitigations.name: Stack Canary
mitigations.primitive_impact: No canary means the crash is not prevented — the corrupted return address is used directly by 'ret'.

evidence.description: PoC: 100 bytes of 'A' as stdin input. Return code = -11 (SIGSEGV). The overflow corrupts the return address with 0x4141414141414141 (from the 'A' padding), which is an unmapped address, causing SIGSEGV when 'ret' attempts to jump there.
PoC: payload = 48*'A' + 8*'B' + 0x4141414141414141. Return code = -11 (SIGSEGV). The return address 0x4141414141414141 is unmapped, confirming the crash is caused by the corrupted return address.

verification_result.details: Two PoC runs confirm CRASH: (1) 100 bytes of 'A' → return_code=-11 (SIGSEGV); (2) 48*'A'+8*'B'+0x4141414141414141 → return_code=-11 (SIGSEGV). Both crash because the corrupted return address (0x4141414141414141) is unmapped. The crash is a direct consequence of the stack buffer overflow corrupting the return address.

primitives.notes: CRASH is the most basic observable effect of the stack buffer overflow. It is a subset of RIP_CONTROL — when the attacker-controlled return address happens to be invalid, the result is a crash rather than controlled execution. Verified with two different payloads, both producing SIGSEGV (return_code=-11).

unresolved.description: Runtime ASLR status for libc/ld-2.31.so not confirmed
unresolved.reason: PIE is disabled so binary base is fixed at 0x400000. Whether libc/ld addresses are randomized depends on kernel ASLR config, which was not confirmed at runtime. This affects the feasibility of redirecting RIP to libc-resident code (e.g., system, one_gadget) but does not affect RIP_CONTROL to binary-resident code (fixed addresses).
unresolved.required_next_step: S4 should inspect /proc/pid/maps at runtime to confirm whether libc is loaded at a predictable or randomized address, which affects ret2libc exploit chain construction.

unresolved.description: Whether a seccomp or other sandbox is active at runtime
unresolved.reason: No seccomp-related symbols in the binary, but an external sandbox cannot be ruled out from static analysis. If seccomp is active, it may constrain what syscalls can be executed after RIP_CONTROL, affecting S4 exploit chain feasibility.
unresolved.required_next_step: S4 should check for active seccomp filters at runtime (e.g., via /proc/pid/status or seccomp-tools) to determine whether control-flow redirection would be constrained.
